en: *Treatise on the Establishment of Karma in the Mahāyāna*, one fascicle.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
In various sūtras, the Blessed One has spoken of three types of karma: namely, bodily karma (*kāyakarma*), vocal karma (*vākkarma*), and mental karma (*manaskarma*).

Regarding these, some say that because it is karma performed by the body, it is called bodily karma; because speech itself is karma, it is called vocal karma. Both of these have informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) matter as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because it is associated with the mind, it is called mental action (*manas-karman*); this action has volition (*cetanā*) alone as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, within this context, what dharma is designated as "informative" (*vijñapti*)?
First, bodily informative action has shape (*saṃsthāna*) as its nature; it is produced by the mind and its concomitants taking that [shape] as their object.
Whose form and color is it that is called the "form and color of the body"?
If it is the form and color of the body, why was it previously stated that because it is karma produced by the body, it is called "bodily karma"?
It is called the "form and color of the body" because, as a part of the whole designated as "body," it is subsumed within that single portion.
Because it arises in dependence upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the body, it is called "produced by the body.
The general term for "body" is also applied to its specific parts, just as in common worldly usage one speaks of "residing in a town" or "dwelling in a forest."
For what reason is it further stated that [speech] is "produced by the mind and so forth which take this as their object"?

It is intended to distinguish it from the shape and color of the lips and so forth; for those are not produced by the mind and so forth which take them as objects, since the mind and so forth arise taking vocal sounds as their objects.

Furthermore, this is to distinguish it from the form produced by the mind and other factors induced by past vows; for that [form] is not produced by the very mind and other factors that serve as its conditions, since it is produced by other minds and factors that act as ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*).
Why is it called "informative" (*vijñapti*)?
Because it can manifest the mind that initiates an action, thereby making it known to others.
To clarify this meaning, a verse is spoken:
Manifesting externally through body and speech, they express what is contemplated within the mind;
it is like a fish dwelling in a deep pool, which reveals its presence by stirring the waves.
What is this "manifest form" (vijñapti-rūpa)?
It refers to the nature of length and so forth.
What is length and so forth?
It refers to the application of the names and concepts of "length" and so forth to those [objects].
In what category is this included?
It is said to be included within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Now, it should be examined:
Are length and so forth distinctions of atoms, just like manifest color?
Or are they an accumulation of distinctions of atoms?
Or are they a separate entity that pervades the collection of color and the other [sensory objects]?
If that were the case, what fault would there be?
If length and so forth were merely distinctions among atoms, then, just as with visible color, length and so forth should be perceivable when each individual atom within a mass of matter is analyzed.
If it were a collection of distinct atoms, what difference would there be between this and a collection of atoms of manifest color?
It follows that the various collections of manifest colors themselves should constitute length and so forth.

If a single distinct entity were to pervade the aggregate of form and so forth, then because it is one and pervasive, it should be fully perceivable within each individual part, since it is present in all parts;
or else it would not be one, as it would reside separately within each of those parts.
Furthermore, this would undermine your own school's tenet that all ten sense bases are merely accumulations of atoms;
it would also force you to side with the proponents of the "rice-grain" doctrine (*taṇḍulavāda*), who maintain that a real part exists pervading all its constituent parts.

Within a composite aggregate of matter, when one sees many [parts] on one side, the cognition of "long" arises; when one sees few [parts] on one side, the cognition of "short" arises; when one sees [parts] equal on all four sides, the cognition of "square" arises; when one sees all sides filled out, the cognition of "round" arises; when one sees a protrusion in the center, the cognition of "high" arises; when one sees a depression in the center, the cognition of "low" arises; when one sees the surface level and even, the cognition of "even" arises; and when one sees the surface uneven, the cognition of "uneven" arises. Just as various cognitions of different shapes arise when observing a wheel being spun or a brocade, it is not the case that distinct types of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) actually exist in the same location in the way that manifest colors (*varṇa-rūpa*) do.
If you were to grant this, then one should give rise to the cognition of all shapes at each and every location.

However, such a thing does not occur; therefore, shape-color has no separate substantial entity. It is simply various manifest colors that, when arranged differently across various directions, give rise to the cognition of "long" and so forth—just as there is no fault in the case of rows of trees or ants.
If that is so, how is it that in a distant, dark place one does not perceive color (varṇa) but perceives shape (saṃsthāna)?
How is it that one cannot perceive the shapes of trees and the like, yet can perceive their arrangement?

However, there is no separate "row" apart from the trees and so forth; or, among various clusters of color-form in the distance or in darkness, one cannot discern either the manifest color or the shape. Although they are apprehended, they are not distinct, leading to the doubt: "What thing is this? What is being seen here?"

From this, it should be understood that one perceives only visible color (*varṇa*); because of distance and darkness, the perception is not distinct. Therefore, the logical argument that the indicative [action] (*vijñapti*) is shape (*saṃsthāna*) is not established. Some say:
"The bodily indicative has movement as its nature; it is produced by the mind and other factors, taking this [movement] as its object."
For what reason is it further stated that [speech] is produced by the mind and other factors taking this as their object?

It is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the movement of the lips and so forth; for those [movements] are not produced by the mind and other factors taking them as objects, since the mind and other factors arise taking the vocal sounds as their objects.
What is meant by "movement"?
It refers to the transition to another location.
In what category is this included?
That is to say, it is subsumed within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
On what basis is it known that this [form] moves to another location?
Because its distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be perceived.

This reasoning is incorrect; for example, in the case of substances undergoing transformation through heating (*pākaja*), although there are differences in the conditions for heating—such as contact with fire, light, snow, or vinegar—the specific characteristics of those differences cannot be perceived.
Nevertheless, there is indeed a difference between its prior and subsequent states; this case should be understood in the same way.

For example, when a large quantity of firewood or grass consists of similar parts, although distinct flames arise from each part with their own differences, those specific differences cannot be discerned.
However, those constituent parts are not without difference; this case should be understood in the same way.

If the characteristics of transformation through heating were not to arise immediately upon contact with the conditions, they would likewise not arise at a later time, because the conditions have not changed.

If the various parts of a long piece of firewood or grass were similar and no flame were produced from each individual part, then that flame would not exist; for it is due to those distinct parts that there are differences in shape, magnitude, illumination, and the heat of the flame.

Therefore, one should not conclude that this very thing moves to another location simply because its distinct characteristics cannot be perceived; rather, one should carefully investigate and understand those distinct characteristics.
If it is argued that because no cause for cessation can be found, one knows that this very phenomenon merely moves to another location—this too is irrational.
For instance, in the case of mind, mental factors, sound, lamp flames, and so forth, what cause for cessation exists such that they cease moment by moment?
The same should apply to other things as well: cessation does not depend on a cause.

If you claim that mental states and the like also have causes for their cessation—namely, their own respective individual characteristics of impermanence—then why do you not allow this to be the case for other things as well?
Since it is not so for other things, how could this be otherwise?
Therefore, one knows that the cessation of mind and its concomitants does not depend on a cause.
As it is with the mind and its concomitants, so it should be with all other things as well.
If other phenomena were to perish without depending on causes, then prior to the contact of fuel and so forth with fire and so forth, their nature as color-form and so forth should be unperceivable;
yet, just as it is in the state after contact, it should likewise be perceivable in the prior state.
How is it that before the wind or hand has touched or grasped the lamp or bell, the flame and the sound are clearly perceivable, whereas they are not so at a later stage?
Furthermore, the extinction of the flame and the sound does not depend on the wind or the hand; the same applies to fuel and other such things, so this should not be raised as an objection.

Furthermore, if the nature of color and so forth were ungraspable when fire and the like extinguish fuel and the like, then it would follow that they should be ungraspable immediately upon contact; for there is a distinction at the very moment of contact, and because those external conditions themselves possess no such distinction.

When various transformed objects—whether inferior, medium, or superior—arise with distinct characteristics of transformation, they arise successively and perish successively, with each preceding state ceasing as each succeeding state arises, due to those [transformations] acting as causes.
What, then, could be the cause?

It is not logical that this phenomenon arises because of that [cause], and yet that very same phenomenon ceases because of that same phenomenon; it is a well-established worldly principle that two mutually contradictory phenomena cannot share a single cause.
Therefore, conditioned phenomena do not depend on a cause of destruction; they perish spontaneously by their own nature.

As previously stated regarding the "graspable" and the "ungraspable," one should understand that within the continuous process of transformation, there is a subtle increase in the characteristics of disintegration and destruction.
Furthermore, if the phenomenon of cessation were also to have a cause, then there would be no such thing as causeless cessation.

Just as the mind and mental factors arise in dependence upon causes, their cessation should likewise be so; for it is not established by common consensus that impermanence exists as something distinct from the mind and its concomitants.
Furthermore, because causes are distinct, cessation should vary accordingly, just as the transformation through heating varies due to the differences between fire, light, snow, vinegar, and so forth.
Moreover, a phenomenon that has already ceased should be subject to further cessation, since you admit it possesses a cause, just like form and other such phenomena.
Therefore, the phenomenon of cessation is definitively without cause.
Because cessation is causeless, it ceases as soon as it arises; thus, one knows that there is no transition to another location.
If it is argued that because a cause for arising cannot be found, one knows that this very phenomenon transitions to another location—[this is not so].

This is also unreasonable because there exists a cause for arising; that is, the preceding acts as the cause for the arising of the succeeding. This is like the preceding moment of mind and the subsequent moment of mind, the preceding transformation of ripening and the subsequent transformation of ripening, milk and its curd, grape juice and wine, and wine and its vinegar. Therefore, not even the slightest phenomenon moves to another location.
Since reciprocal transformation is absent, how can there be movement?
Furthermore, if there were abiding, there would be no movement; since there is no movement, it should be eternally constant.
If a phenomenon lacks abiding, it likewise lacks movement, for it perishes as soon as it arises, being devoid of the meaning of motion.
If that is so, what is it that we actually perceive when seeing motion?
It is not the same original object as seen in another location.
On what grounds do we know that it is not the original object?
Because it arises anew in each respective location, it is like the flame of a grass fire or like the movement of a shadow.

It is not that the form and substance of a shadow in one place can be seen in another place while remaining stationary; rather, as the light of the sun and other sources revolves at varying distances, one perceives those shadows as being long or short, or as shifting from place to place.
Furthermore, because it obstructs even a small portion of the arising of light,
there is a counter-interrogation:
"For what reason is the argument of reaching other locations being raised?"
Furthermore, how do we know that what is seen in other locations is not the very same original object?
This too should be proven by invoking the preceding reasoning: namely, that if something were to abide, it could not move, and so forth.
Furthermore, although external conditions such as fire and so forth do not differ, a difference can be perceived at a later time; by this it is proven that [the object] is distinct in each moment.
Moreover, if one were to claim that what is seen subsequently is still the same original object because no cause for its alteration has been established, [that would be a fallacy].
Since there is no cause [for the change], and the proof is that it is the very same object, for what reason do you not say it is not the original object?
Consequently, because these two points are both indeterminate, the argument does not hold when applied to other locations.
The Sūryodayavādins (Proponents of the Rising Sun) speak as follows:
"There is no reality to the notion that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) travel to other locations, because the nature of conditioned things is such that they perish moment by moment.

Nevertheless, there exists a distinct phenomenon caused by mental differentiation, which arises in dependence upon the hands, feet, and so forth; this phenomenon is capable of producing the objects known as hands, feet, and the like."
The cause for arising in a different location is called "motion" (gati) and is also termed "bodily intimation" (kāyavijñapti).
Under which category is this subsumed?
It is subsumed under the sphere of form (rūpāyatana).
If that is so, for what reason do you not admit that the eye sees [it] just as it sees various manifest colors (*varṇa*)?
Since it is not something seen and does not indicate anything else, how can it be called "indicative" (*vijñapti*)?
Furthermore, how is it known that this dharma truly exists?
How is it that this dharma causes the body itself to move toward another location and arise in a different state?
If you say it is due to a particularity of the mind, then the wind element produced thereby should likewise be so.
The nature of the wind element is motion; it alone is capable of acting as the cause for the arising [of things] in different locations.
Why, then, do you abandon the wind and maintain that there is a separate dharma of motion?
Furthermore, since grass, leaves, and the like lack any distinct dharma of motion apart from the external wind element, how could they be displaced?

However, since the various wind elements arise from shaking, contact, and so forth, and their nature is to move, one should simply admit that they cause the hands and other limbs to be produced in different locations; why labor to maintain a separate [substantial] entity?
Whether in terms of essence or function, neither is established as a moving dharma that produces [motion].

If this were not the case, then the wind element produced by a particular state of mind, which serves as the cause for the hand and so forth to arise in different locations, would have to be bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
Thus, the wind element has no representation; how then can it be called "representation"?
Furthermore, if you admit that the sphere of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana) is either wholesome or unwholesome, then you are not a son of the Śākya.

If this were not the case, then since the differentiation of the mind can cause one's own body to arise in another location, that very arising of the body should be bodily representation (kāyavijñapti).
In that case, bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) would have to be nominal rather than real, because it consists of a composite body of many dharmas.
Furthermore, since there is no actual communication, how can it be called "intimation"?
For odors and the like cannot communicate anything to others.
Furthermore, if one were to admit that odors and so forth are wholesome or unwholesome, one would no longer be a son of the Śākya.

If this were not the case, then the visible form produced by a particular state of mind should be the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*); however, visible form is not produced by a particular state of mind, because it arises from the differentiation of its own seeds and wind.
Furthermore, if one admits that visible form (*varṇa*) is either wholesome or unwholesome, then one is no longer a son of the Śākya.
If this visible form does not have the body as its substance for manifestation, then its arising in another location must be what constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).

Devānāmpriya, you may exert all your power and apply yourself with diligent effort toward this manifest karma; however, this cannot be accomplished through the application of effort—why then do you labor in vain over it?
Who can establish that arising has a separate substantial entity?
This "arising" as you conceive it is not something visible like form and so forth, nor is it something capable of seeing like the eye and so forth; by what means, then, is its existence known?
Furthermore, it is invisible; how then can it be called "informative" (*vijñapti*)?
As stated previously, it cannot represent itself to others.
Moreover, if the manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*) were itself wholesome or unwholesome, one could say that its production constitutes bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karman*).
However, since it has already been stated that visible forms (*varṇa*) are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, the same must apply to arising (*jāti*).
Therefore, there certainly exists no real bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karman*).
If this is so, then bodily karma would consist solely of the non-informative (*avijñapti*).
To what phenomenon does this term "unmanifest" (avijñapti) refer?
It refers to the matter of the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana-saṃgṛhīta-rūpa), such as the discipline of restraint (saṃvara).
How can there be wholesome unmanifest karma in the desire realm that arises independently of manifest action (vijñapti)?
If this unmanifest (avijñapti) were to exist within the desire realm, what fault would there be?
It would have to follow the mind, just as it does in the form realm.
Consequently, during other states of mind or in the state of no-mind, there would be no discipline (saṃvara) or non-discipline (asaṃvara), and so forth.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because at the time of receiving [the precepts], speech is prompted by a prior commitment (*samaya*), then how could one incur the offense of false speech when remaining silent and making no commitment during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra?
Furthermore, there would be no indeterminate bodily karma, because non-informative karma (avijñapti) exists in only two types [wholesome and unwholesome].
Moreover, there would be no wholesome or unwholesome bodily karma for even a single moment, because all non-informative karma is necessarily continuous.

That is to say, if a light mind does not give rise to non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), whereas that which is produced by a heavy mind necessarily continues in a stream, then even if one were to conceptually impute that bodily and vocal karma exists as a substantial form (*rūpa*), it could not logically constitute the nature of being wholesome or unwholesome.

Why is this so? Because they assert that at the moment of death, all karmic formations of form (*rūpa-karman*) must necessarily be relinquished; how, then, could these result in future desirable or undesirable fruits?
Some say: Why is this not reasonable?
It is because past karma exists as a real entity, capable of bringing about the fruits to be experienced in the future.

This is like developing a further abscess upon an existing one: namely, to insist that the substance of past karma exists in reality. Since "the past" is defined as that which previously existed but now no longer does, how can its substance be maintained to exist in reality?
If that is so, for what reason did the Blessed One himself say:
"Though karma may pass through a hundred eons, it never perishes;
when it encounters the convergence of various conditions, it must inevitably yield its fruit"?
What meaning does the phrase "without loss or destruction" (*avipraṇāśa*) clarify?
It clarifies that the karma one performs is not without fruit; this meaning is established by the latter half of the verse.
Who would not believe and accept that wholesome and unwholesome karma, even after passing through a long duration, is able to yield its fruit?
One should merely investigate how the fruit is obtained:
is it obtained through a specific transformation within the continuum, as in the case of a rice seed and so forth?
Or is it obtained because the self-characteristic remains intact and persists for a long duration before yielding the fruit?
If the fruit is obtained through a specific transformation within the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*), then this principle may well be acceptable.

However, if it were obtained while the action itself remains intact for a long period of time by virtue of its own intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), then one would have to say that this action, without its essence having perished over a long period of time, is able to produce the fruit.

If it is claimed that this karma does not cease because its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is non-existent, but rather ceases because it no longer possesses functional activity (kāritra), then how is it that this karma no longer possesses functional activity?
Because it can no longer project a future fruit.
For what reason can it no longer project a future fruit?
Because that fruit has already been projected by this [action] in the past.
A fruit cannot be projected again after it has already been projected, just as a dharma that has already arisen does not arise again.
For what reason does it not project other results of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*)?
Because results of uniform outflow have no temporal limit; for is this result not also present at that time?
Since it has already been cited, there is no need to cite it again. If the substance of karma does not perish and must always be present, why does it not constantly project its resulting fruit?

Is it not true that we previously stated that once a fruit has been projected, it cannot be projected again—just as a dharma that has already arisen does not arise again? Why, then, do you raise this objection once more?
Although there was previously a statement, the objection has not yet been resolved.
If the substance of karma were eternally existent, it should—like its middle phase—be constantly designated as "present";
and since it would always be capable of projecting a fruit, it should—like its initial phase—be perpetually subject to arising once again.
If it is argued that although the substance of past karma exists, it is not present because it lacks activity, and because it is not present, it cannot project a fruit—this is also incorrect;
since its substance is eternally present, it should, like the present, eternally possess activity.
Furthermore, according to your own tenet, past phenomena possess the function of giving fruit; why then are they not considered present?

If you argue that the term "present" applies only to the function of grasping fruit (*phalagrahaṇa*) of phenomena, this reasoning is also incorrect, because since the meaning of "function" is the same, both [functions] should be equally present.

If past phenomena are called "past" because they lack the function of taking up a fruit (*phala*), then they should be called "present" when they possess the function of giving a fruit (*phala*). Furthermore, when this function is exhausted, they should be called "extinguished. In that case, phenomena would undergo extinction after having already been extinguished; likewise, they would also have to arise after having already arisen. Therefore, the tenets of that school are not logically established.
Furthermore, in what sense is it called "able to project a fruit"?
It means establishing that [fruit] so that it shall arise in the future.
For one whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*), the final momentary state should not project a fruit, because nothing further arises thereafter.
In that case, this thought would not be present; it should not further cease and enter the past.
Since it already lacks functional activity at the initial moment of being present, how can it be said to "pass away" at a later time?
If something were to be extinguished again even though it is already without function, then that which has passed would likewise have to be extinguished again.
If what has already been extinguished were to be extinguished once more, then what has already arisen would have to arise again; this would entail a contradiction of the faults previously stated.
If it is argued that although this thought possesses the capacity to produce a subsequent result, the result does not arise because conditions are lacking—this too is irrational;
for if the result necessarily does not arise, how can one know that there exists a capacity to produce it?

One should say that because this mental state exists or does not exist depending on two conditions—those that are favorable or unfavorable—it lacks the functional capacity to produce a subsequent fruit despite being born from causes.
Therefore, the logical principle of "the capacity to project a fruit" as asserted by that school is necessarily untenable.
Therefore, it should be understood that [the cause] is called "able to project the fruit" simply because it can nourish the seeds of the fruit.
Furthermore, since that school asserts that the substance of both the past and the future is substantially real, why is the future not able to project the fruit in the same manner as the present?
If all things existed at all times, there would never be a time or a thing whose essence did not exist;
yet the Sūtra says:
"When the assembly of various conditions is encountered, it shall repay that fruit."

Furthermore, they should explain: at what stage, with respect to whom, and by what means does one have the capacity [to project]? It is said that establishing something so that it will arise is called "projecting a fruit" (*phalākṣepa*).

Since [if their view were true] everything would exist at all times, the claim that past karma exists as a substantial entity capable of obtaining a future result to be experienced cannot logically be established.

If that is so, one must admit that within the continuum of the aggregates of bodily and vocal actions—whether wholesome or unwholesome—a distinct dharma arises; its substance is truly existent and it is subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra-skandha*).
Some say this dharma is called "increase" (*upacaya*);
others say it is called "non-disappearance" (*avipraṇāśa*). It is by means of this dharma that one is able to obtain future desirable or undesirable fruits.
One must also admit that mental karma possesses this quality; for if it were otherwise, it would be severed when other states of mind arise.
If such a distinct dharma were not produced within the continuum of the mind, how could it possibly obtain its fruit in a future life?
Therefore, one must certainly admit that such a phenomenon exists.
If, having previously studied and mastered the words and meanings of a text, one later recollects them after a long interval;

or if, having previously repeatedly seen, heard, or otherwise perceived various objects, one later recollects those very objects after a long interval—then at which moment is what phenomenon produced, by virtue of which there arises this subsequent recollection?

Furthermore, what phenomenon is produced by the mind that first enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth, such that at a later time, one emerges from that absorption and produces the mind of emergence?
Moreover, when lac dye colors a citron flower, both of those [the dye and the flower] perish; what phenomenon is produced by them such that, when the fruit later ripens, its pulp becomes red?

Therefore, apart from those [schools] that postulate a distinct dharma induced by the two types of action—bodily and vocal—one must hold that it is solely through the specific activity of volition (*cetanā*) that the mental continuum is perfumed, causing a functional capacity to arise; and through the transformation of this capacity into a particular state, the various fruits of future lives are produced.

Just as the juice of lac dyes a citron flower, which undergoes a continuous transformation until the time the fruit ripens and its pulp becomes red, one should know that the internal dharmas of perfuming are likewise.
Furthermore, why not allow that the two types of action—bodily and vocal—infuse the mental continuum?
This is because bodily and vocal actions are established as virtuous or non-virtuous by being induced by the mind.

It is not the case that what is established as virtuous or non-virtuous by the mind could produce future desirable or undesirable fruits within a different continuum; for it is not the case that one person performs the action while another receives the fruit.

If it is the case that although the substance of a performed action has perished, one can still obtain future results such as pleasure through a specific transformation of the functional capacity within the continuum of the perfumed mind, then how can prior karma produce future desirable or undesirable fruits when the mental continuum is severed during the attainment of the mindless meditative absorptions (*acittaka-samāpatti*) or among the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*)?
Some say: Within this present life, the mind previously perfumed must necessarily continue its succession; therefore, one obtains future fruits, whether pleasant or unpleasant.
Since it has already been interrupted, by what cause can it be reconnected?

If it is argued that the mind entering meditative absorption (*samāhita-citta*) acts as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and thus enables the subsequent continuity, then how can that mind, having long since ceased and perished, act as an equal-and-immediate condition?

This case is identical to the refutation of past karma being able to yield a fruit; it should be refuted in the same manner through correct reasoning. Therefore, the mind emerging from absorption should not arise as a continuous succession.

Some say: By the power of the seeds dependent upon the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), the subsequent mind arises again; for the seeds capable of producing the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) rely upon two continuities—namely, the continuity of mind and the continuity of the material sense-faculties—according to what is appropriate.
Does not the Sūtra state:
"With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises"?
How could mental consciousness arise apart from the mind?

One should understand that the mental seeds are sometimes called "mind" because the name of the effect is applied to the cause, just as the names "hunger" and "thirst" are applied to the objects of touch.
How can each individual mind and mental factor arise from two seed-continuities?
It is not observed that there is such a phenomenon as sprouts and so forth arising from seeds, wherein a single fruit could be produced by relying upon multiple conditions;
nor is it the case that a single fruit arises from two types of seeds.
If that were so, one would still not avoid the aforementioned fault:
namely, since the mental continuum is severed in the mindless attainments and among the gods of the realm of non-conception, how could prior karma produce future desirable or undesirable fruits?
This is a fault in that school's tenet.
What is meant by "that school"?
It refers to those who maintain that this state is entirely devoid of mind.
If it is asserted that this state possesses consciousness, then this fault does not arise.
As stated in the *Paryāyapada-śāstra* composed by the Venerable Vasumitra:
"If one maintains that the attainment of cessation is entirely devoid of consciousness, then this fault would indeed exist."
I maintain that even in the meditative attainment of cessation there remains a subtle mind; therefore, this fault does not apply.
They further cite a sutra to establish this point, as it is said in the scripture:
"For one abiding in the attainment of cessation, all bodily formations are extinguished," and so on at length, until: "the sense faculties do not undergo disintegration."
Consciousness does not depart from the body; what consciousness, then, is admitted to exist in this state? Some say:
"There is the sixth mental consciousness (manovijñāna)."
Is it not stated in the Sūtra:
"With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises; the coming together of these three is contact; and with contact, feeling, perception, and volition arise simultaneously"?

How could it be that in this state there is mental consciousness without the coming together of the three, or the coming together of the three without contact, or contact without feeling and perception?
For this reason, it is called the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Some offer this explanation:
"How is it that the Blessed One said 'feeling conditions craving,' yet not all feelings serve as conditions for craving?"
Contact (*sparśa*) should also be understood in this way; not all contact serves as a condition for feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors].

In another sutra, the Blessed One himself clarified this point, stating that "the various feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-sparśaja-vedanā*) serve as the condition for the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*)."
There is no instance where contact gives rise to sensation without such discrimination; therefore, that [explanation] is not a sound interpretation.
Another explanation states:
"The contact of the threefold harmony" means that because the three factors possess power and conjoin, contact arises.

In this state, the three factors lack the power to produce contact (*sparśa*) or to give rise to feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), because they have been suppressed by the mind that has entered meditative absorption.

Since even contact does not exist while one is actually in the state of absorption, how much less could there be feeling and perception? Therefore, in this state, only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) remains, devoid of all mental concomitants (*caitta*).
If that is so, what is the nature of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) at this stage?
Is it wholesome, defiled, or neutral (*avyākṛta*)?
If such were the case, what fault would there be?
If it is of a wholesome nature, how can that which is of a wholesome nature not be associated with the wholesome roots such as non-attachment?
Even if it were associated with the wholesome roots such as non-attachment, how could it be without contact?

If it is argued that this consciousness is virtuous because it is induced by a virtuous immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), this is logically untenable, because a virtuous mind can be followed immediately by three types of minds.
Furthermore, there is no cause capable of obstructing the wholesome mind induced by the power of the roots of goodness, because it is free from greed and the other [unwholesome roots].
Moreover, if it lacked the roots of goodness, it would not constitute a wholesome state.
However, this meditative attainment of cessation is wholesome, just as its cessation is wholesome.
If it were of the nature of defilement, how could that which is of the nature of defilement not be associated with afflictions such as greed?
And even if it were associated with afflictions such as greed, how could it be without contact?
As the Buddha himself stated in that *Daśapraśna-sūtra*:
"All aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) have contact (*sparśa*) as their condition."
Furthermore, since even the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is not admitted to be defiled, how much less so the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)!

If it were of the nature of non-obscured-neutral (anivṛta-avyākṛta), would it be born of maturation (vipākaja), or of deportment (airyāpathika), or of craftsmanship (śailpasthānika), or of supernormal transformation (nairmāṇika)?
If that were the case, what fault would there be?

If it were produced by maturation (*vipākaja*), how could a mind of maturation belonging to the desire realm arise immediately after a meditative mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), when the eight intermediate stages [of the form realm] are so vastly separated?
How, moreover, can the immovable mind (*āniñjya-citta*) and other such minds manifest immediately after this [mind]?
As it is asked in the Mahākauṣṭhila Sūtra: "When emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), how many contacts (*sparśa*) does one experience?"
He replied: "Venerable, one should experience three contacts:
namely, the contact of imperturbability, the contact of nothingness, and the contact of signlessness."
Furthermore, what is the principle by which the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*), though projected by past karma,
is constrained such that its limit for emerging from meditative absorption does not exceed the time previously determined before entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?
Furthermore, for what reason?

It is because the mind that reaches its ultimate limit—having the cessation [of suffering] at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as its object—is induced by the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) of past actions in the desire realm; only then does the resultant ripened consciousness (*vipākaphala-citta*) arise, and not in any prior stage.

Furthermore, for what reason does the matter produced by maturation (*vipākaja-rūpa*) not continue once it has been severed, whereas the mind produced by maturation continues even after being severed?

And if [the mind] pertains to the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), or the power of transformation (*nairmāṇika*), how can this mind, taking the modes of deportment and so forth as its objects, perform various actions without the presence of contact (*spraṣṭavya*)?

Furthermore, since it is accepted that the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*) and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) cultivated therein are all wholesome in nature, it would be illogical for an afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind to manifest during these stages.

Furthermore, by taking cessation as its object within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and relying upon the meditative concentration of the contemplation of tranquility, one is then able to manifest entry into the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
As stated in the Mahākauṣṭhila Sūtra, regarding the meditative attainment of cessation, it asks:
"By how many causes and by how many conditions, relying upon what, is one able to enter the concentration of the signless (*animitta-samādhi*)?"

He replied: "Venerable, there are two causes and two conditions upon which one relies to enter the concentration of the signless realm: namely, not conceptualizing any signs and correctly contemplating the signless realm."
If there were mental consciousness within the attainment of cessation, what would its object be,
and what would its mode of activity be?
If it took cessation as its object and operated with a mode of activity characterized by tranquility, how could it not be wholesome?
If this is considered wholesome, why is it not admitted to be associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment?
And even if such association were admitted, why is it not admitted that contact (*sparśa*) functions as its condition?

If one were to take other objects as focal points and form other mental aspects, how could it be that a distracted mind arises immediately after the mind entering the meditative attainment of cessation without contradicting reason?
Even if one were to speculate that there exists some other neutral state, for these two reasons, such a view would likewise be unreasonable.

Therefore, you do not understand the meaning of the Āgamas as they truly are; you recklessly and falsely imagine that the sixth consciousness exists in states such as the meditative absorption of cessation, and on this basis, you maintain that there is mind in these states.
If that is so, how can you maintain that there is still mind during the various mindless states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

You should accept, just as those for whom certain sūtras are authoritative do, that a subtle mind still exists in those states. This refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) which possesses all seeds; from the initial moment of conception until death, it continues in a successive stream without ever being interrupted. In various places of birth, it flows on through the succession of its own maturing causes and specific categories, until it finally ceases utterly at *nirvāṇa*.

Precisely because this consciousness is uninterrupted, it is said that there is "mind" even during states of non-mentation; since the other six groups of consciousness do not function in these various states, they are described as being "without mind."

Due to the predominant power of the mind entering through the preparatory application of the attainment of cessation and so forth, the seeds of the six consciousnesses are temporarily suppressed and prevented from manifesting; therefore, it is called "mindless," not because all [consciousness] is absent.
The mind is of two kinds:
first, the mind that accumulates and arises, because it is the locus where immeasurable seeds accumulate and arise;
second, the mind of manifold variety, because it evolves through the distinctions of objective referents and modes of activity.

In states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is called "mindless" because the second moment of mind is absent, just as a bed with only one leg is called "legless" because it lacks the remaining legs.

In those states where the seeds of the various consciousnesses have been suppressed, the resultant ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) undergoes moment-to-moment transformation and differentiation. The power capable of suppressing them gradually weakens and diminishes until it is completely exhausted, just as the power that draws forth heat from a heated arrow gradually weakens and diminishes until it reaches the state of total exhaustion.

At that time, the seeds of consciousness obtain the opportunity to produce their fruit; first, from the seeds of consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises again, and subsequently, depending on conditions, the other consciousnesses gradually emerge. This is precisely what was previously described as the ripening-result consciousness (*vipākaphala-vijñāna*), which contains and stores the seeds of all various phenomena.

When those various other consciousnesses and their concomitant factors, being wholesome or unwholesome in nature, repeatedly perfume and activate [the seeds], the power of the seeds increases accordingly as appropriate; through this, there occurs a transformation and differentiation within the continuum.
According to the power of the seeds sown and upon encountering auxiliary conditions, one then experiences the results of future desirable or undesirable fruits.
Based on this principle, it is said in a verse:
The mind, together with boundless seeds, Continues in a perpetual stream.
When encountering various distinct conditions for perfuming, the seeds of the mind increase and flourish.
As the power of these seeds gradually ripens, they yield their fruit when conditions converge;
it is like the *bījapūra* flower, whose pulp becomes red at the time of fruition.
Based on this, the Blessed One spoke these verses in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Mahāyāna Sūtra*:
"The ādānavijñāna is profound and subtle; Containing all seeds, it is like a turbulent stream.
I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, Fearing they would conceptually grasp it as a self."
Because it can continue future existence and can maintain the body, it is called the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
Because it gathers and stores the seeds of all phenomena, it is further called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Because it is the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma projected in previous lives, this very consciousness is also called the "maturation-consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*).
If one does not admit the existence of this maturation-consciousness, what other consciousness could possibly maintain and uphold the body?
It is not that another consciousness can pervasively maintain the body, for [the storehouse consciousness] does not abandon it until the end of life.
Furthermore, at what point could the arising of the antidote to the latent afflictions within the aggregates be termed "able to sever"?
If it is claimed that the aggregates reside in the mind that acts as their antidote, this is unreasonable: how could latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) that persist [with the mind] serve as its antidote?

Furthermore, when sentient beings born in the formless realm give rise to a defiled, wholesome, or untainted mind, what karmically matured (*vipāka*) phenomena belonging to any destiny (*gati*) could possibly exist therein?
Alternatively, one would have to admit that the destinies (gati) include both non-retributive and non-bound phenomena, which would contradict reason.
Furthermore, when an Anāgāmin is born in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), he cultivates the path of counteraction in order to exhaust the remaining outflows (āsrava).

When the untainted state arises in the sphere of nothingness, what distinct entity remains in its own nature within the Peak of Existence that is not termed "death" and does not constitute a separate homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*)?
Alternatively, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) might be considered a distinct substantial entity apart from form, mind, and so forth;
however, these two [the life-faculty and the faculty of mind] are merely conventionally established upon the similar momentum within the various aggregates of maturation (vipāka).

Similarity in functional capacity has no separate substantial entity, just as the similarity in functional capacity between rice and weeds does not. Therefore, one must certainly admit that there exists a seed-holding consciousness, distinct from the six groups of consciousness, with the nature described above.

Based on this very consciousness, the Theravāda scriptures establish the name "bhavanga-consciousness," the Mahāsāṃghika scriptures name it "root-consciousness" (mūlavijñāna), and the Mahīśāsaka school speaks of it as the "aggregate that persists until the end of saṃsāra."
What is the mode of activity (*ākāra*) by which this consciousness perceives its objects? This mode of activity cannot be discerned.
How is it that what is called "consciousness" can be thus?

Just as it is difficult to know the objects and modes of activity of consciousness when one maintains that some form of consciousness persists during states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), so too should this [consciousness] be understood.
Within which of the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) is this consciousness included?
In truth, it should be stated that it is subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
If this is so, how are the scriptural passages to be reconciled?
For example, as it is said:
What is called the aggregate of appropriation consisting of consciousness?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness.
Furthermore, it is said:
How is it that consciousness conditions name-and-form?
"Consciousness" refers to the six consciousnesses.
One should understand that this sutra has a specific underlying intention (*abhiprāya*), as stated in another sutra:
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?
It refers to the six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ-cetanā-kāya*).
There are no other dharmas within the aggregate of formations; this [case] should be understood in the same way.
What is the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) for teaching six [consciousnesses] and no more?

For instance, as the Blessed One stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*: "I do not reveal this to the foolish and ignorant," because he feared they would conceptually construct and cling to it as a self (*ātman*).
For what reason do foolish commoners cling to this as a self?
Because it has existed from beginningless time until the end of saṃsāra, its mode of activity is subtle and unchanging.

Furthermore, because the six consciousnesses have coarse and easily discernible bases, objects, modes of activity, and categories; because they are associated with the various afflictions and their antidotes; and because they establish the categories of defilement and purification.
The substance [of these six] is resultant consciousness; from this, one infers that there exists a causal consciousness.

Since the various sūtras do not explicitly mention a causal consciousness in accordance with what they proclaim, it would contradict all that has been stated above. Therefore, this is called the "intentional meaning" (*saṃdhi*) of teaching the six [consciousnesses] and no others.

By this, the fact that other schools’ sūtras speak only of the six bodies of consciousness as the *bhavāṅgavijñāna* (life-constituent consciousness) and so forth is already explained; in each case, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, at the present time, immeasurable sūtras within each school have already been lost, as should be understood from the extensive discussion in the *Vyākhyāyukti*. Therefore, one should not maintain that the *ālayavijñāna* is certainly not taught in the sūtras, for it must necessarily exist according to reason.

If that were so, a single body would have to possess two consciousnesses functioning simultaneously—namely, the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
What fault would there be in this?

If two consciousnesses were to function simultaneously within a single body, it would follow that two sentient beings must exist within that one body at the same time, just as when two consciousnesses function simultaneously in different bodies.
There is no such fault here, because the two consciousnesses—cause and effect—serve as mutual supports for one another and are not dissociated.

Furthermore, since the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is perfumed by the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), such a phenomenon does not occur when two consciousnesses evolve simultaneously within different bodies; therefore, this fault does not exist.
Is there any instance observed where the seed and the continuity of its fruit are different?

We observe in the world that for blue lotuses and the like, the roots, stems, and so forth form a distinct continuity from the seed yet constitute its fruit; this case should be understood in the same way.

Furthermore, whether or not it is perceived by the world, if the existence of the ālayavijñāna were not admitted, the aforementioned faults and difficulties would ensue; therefore, one must certainly admit that the ālayavijñāna exists as a substantial entity distinct from the sixfold group of consciousnesses.
For what reason do you not admit that the self-substance exists substantially as the support for the six consciousnesses?
What are the characteristics of the self as you conceive it, such that you say it can serve as the support for the six consciousnesses?

If you grant that the self arises and ceases in a continuous succession, transforming according to conditions just like the *ālayavijñāna*, how does it differ from consciousness such that you insist on calling it the "self"?

If you maintain that the essence of the self is unitary, permanent, and ultimately unchanging, how can you say that it serves as the substratum for being perfumed by sensations, consciousness, and so forth?

Now, as for perfuming (*vāsanā*), it causes the continuum of that which is perfumed to undergo transformation into a specific functional capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*), just as the juice of lacquerwood perfumes a citron flower, causing its continuum to undergo a transformation of functional capacity.
If there were no perfuming (*vāsanā*), there would be no capacity for transformational differentiation.
How then could there be the prior experience of wisdom, desire, and so forth?
Because of the repeated practice of these diverse states, after a long period of time, distinct arisings of recollection, wisdom, desire, and so forth occur.

Furthermore, since the self-essence is no different during the state of mindlessness than it is at a later time, if consciousness is currently absent, from what would the subsequent mental consciousness and other faculties arise?
Moreover, what capacity does the self possess regarding consciousness and the like, that you should insist upon the self as their support?

If it is claimed that consciousness and the other aggregates arise because of a self, and since the essence of the self is eternally without differentiation, how is it that consciousness and the others arise sequentially rather than all arising simultaneously at once?

If you claim that [the self] can only produce [cognition] by depending on the assistance of other causes and conditions, then apart from those other causes and conditions, how can one know that the self possesses the functional capacity to produce?

If you say that consciousness and so forth revolve in dependence upon the self, since all phenomena perish immediately after they arise and thus lack the meaning of "abiding," how could there be any such revolution?
Therefore, one should not maintain that the self-substance exists as a reality to serve as the support for the six consciousnesses.

Furthermore, to maintain the existence of a self contradicts the Āgamas, which state that all phenomena are devoid of self. Thus, the singular, permanent, and real self you maintain is entirely devoid of valid reasoning and is merely a product of deluded sentiment.

By this it is proven that it is solely through the simultaneous perfuming of the distinctions of volition (*cetanā*) that the ālayavijñāna causes its own continuity to undergo a specific transformation, thereby being able to project future results—whether pleasant or unpleasant—which is not like the characteristics of bodily and vocal karma as described by them.
If one does not admit the existence of the two types of action—bodily and vocal—how could one possibly misinterpret the sūtra on the three types of action?
One cannot misinterpret it; rather, one can explain this sūtra according to its true meaning so that it remains free from fault.
How can this sutra be explained without error?
One should eliminate the poison of dogmatic attachment; I shall now explain it in detail.
Why does the sutra state that there are three types of karma?
What is this body? What is action? In what sense is it called "body"?
In what sense is it called "action" (*karman*)?
Furthermore, in what sense are they called "bodily action," "vocal action," and "mental action"?
The question is likewise [to be applied] here.
Furthermore, for what reason does the *sūtra* speak only of the three types of action—bodily and so forth—and not those of the eye and so on?

Why does the *sūtra* teach these three actions? It is to show that the three actions encompass the ten paths of action (*karmapatha*), thereby encouraging those who fear performing too much; it is like the brief teaching of the three trainings given to the son of the Buddha-ṛṣi (Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana).

There are those who maintain that all karma is created solely by the body, and not by speech or mind; in order to demonstrate that these two also have that which they create, the three types of karma are taught.
"Body" refers to the distinct entity formed by the conjunction of the sense faculties and the great elements.
Karma is volition (*cetanā*), which has differentiation as its nature.
That which is formed through accumulation is the meaning of "body" (*kāya*), because it is formed by the accumulation of great derived atoms (*mahābhūta-paramāṇu*).
Some say that the meaning of "body" is the accumulation of various impure things, because the body is the locus for various impure substances.
If that were so, the celestial realm would have no bodies.
The meaning of "karma" (action) is that which is performed according to the intention of the agent.
Volition capable of moving the body is designated as "bodily karma."
Volition (*cetanā*) is of three kinds:
first, deliberative volition; second, determinative volition; and third, impelling volition.
If volition is capable of moving the body, it is designated as bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
This volition is able to induce the cause for the continuity of the body to arise in another location because it gives rise to the wind element.

It should properly be called "action that moves the body," but by omitting the word "move," it is simply termed "bodily action" (*kāyakarman*). This is just as oil that increases strength is called "strength-oil," or wind that moves dust is called "dust-wind"; this case is likewise.
Among the ten paths of action, the first three are admitted to be comprised within bodily action—namely, killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.
How is it that these are designated as "mental karma" (cetanā-karma)?
Because this volitional karma (*cetanā-karman*) can move the body, causing one to commit killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;

the power of volition moves the body to perform an action, which is thus termed "volitional action" (*cetanā-kṛta*). This is as it is said in the world: "mad bandits burned the village, the firewood and grass cooked the rice."
Furthermore, how is volition (cetanā) designated as a "path of action" (karmapatha)?

Because volition involves purposeful activity, it is called "action" (karman); furthermore, because it serves as the path leading to the happy and miserable realms, and because it universally brings about rebirth therein, it receives the name "path of action."
Alternatively, the body that is moved constitutes the path of action of volition (*cetanā-karmapatha*), because the three types of volitional action proceed in dependence upon it.

Furthermore, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct arise from volitional action and are produced by means of the body; thus, in accordance with worldly convention, they are also called bodily actions (*kāyakarman*).

However, these are in reality neither virtuous nor non-virtuous in nature; their names are merely established according to worldly convention. It is so that people in the world may rely on this gateway to diligently cultivate the performance and avoidance of virtuous and non-virtuous volitions; therefore, they are conventionally designated by the names "virtuous" and "non-virtuous."
If it were only volitional karma that is wholesome or unwholesome, why does the *Karmapatha-sūtra* state:
"Because of the three types of bodily [karma], intentional karma is performed and accumulated; being unwholesome, it can produce bitter fruits and bitter maturation?"

The meaning of this sutra is as follows: that which can move the body, takes the body as its gateway, and takes the body as its basis; having killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as its objects, and volitional karma (*cetanā-karman*) as its cause, it is capable of producing the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of suffering. These are called the three types of bodily [karma], and thus one intentionally creates karma through the body.
Apart from this, other volitions (*cetanā*) are termed mental action (*manas-karman*), because they are associated with the mind and are incapable of setting in motion either body or speech.
If that is so, for what reason does the Sūtra state:
"There are two types of action, namely, the action of volition (*cetana-karman*) and the action after having willed (*cetayitvā-karman*)"?

Among the three types of volition previously mentioned, the first two types are termed "volitional action" (cetanā-karman), while the third single type is termed "action subsequent to volition" (cetayitvā-karman); thus, there is no contradiction with the sūtras.
Speech refers to verbal expression; its nature is sound. Because it can manifest the meaning intended to be expressed, it is called "speech.
The volition that initiates speech is termed "vocal action" (vāg-karman).
Alternatively, "speech" (*vāc*) is that upon which syllables and so forth depend; because it expresses meaning by carrying those syllables and so forth, it is called speech.
In full, one should say "the activity of producing speech," but by omitting the word "producing," it is simply termed "verbal action" (*vākkarman*), as explained by the previous analogy.
"Mind" (manas) refers to consciousness, because it is capable of deliberation.
Because it moves toward future births and toward objects, it is called "mind.
The mental activity that initiates movement is called "mental karma" (manas-karma), as it causes the mind to perform various deeds, such as those that are wholesome or unwholesome.
It should properly be called "the action of attention" (*manasikāra-karman*); by omitting the word "attention," it is simply termed "mental action.
Alternatively, an action associated with the mind is called "mental action"; by omitting the word "associated," it is simply termed "mental action. The explanation through analogy is as before.

If the three types of karma have volition alone as their essence, then during states of distracted mind or the state of non-consciousness (acittaka), since there is no volition at those times, how could one be said to possess restraint (saṃvara) or non-restraint (asaṃvara)?
Because the seeds perfumed by specific volitions (*cetanā-viśeṣa*) remain undestroyed, one is said to be "endowed with restraint" or "endowed with non-restraint"; thus, there is no fault.
"Specific volition" refers to the selection of superior volitions capable of producing the informative acts (*vijñapti*) of restraint or non-restraint.

Due to this volition, two kinds of superior seeds are perfumed; based on these two seeds while they remain in an undestroyed state, the non-informative [karma] of wholesome and unwholesome restraint is provisionally established.
How can it be said that [the seeds] are thus damaged by the differentiation of volition?
It means that from this point onward, they no longer function as causes for the arising of either obstructed or unobstructed volitions.
Who can destroy such seeds as were previously received?

It is said that if there is volition capable of manifesting informative action (*vijñapti*), one thereby abandons wholesome or unwholesome restraints (*saṃvara*); furthermore, other causes of abandonment are likewise able to destroy them.

The reason why the activities of the eye and so forth are not mentioned is that this sutra speaks only of the karma of sentient beings' volitional application (*prayoga*), and does not speak of the functional activity (*kāritra*) of dharmas.
What is meant by the karma of volitional application of sentient beings?
It refers to that which is performed in accordance with the intention of the agent.
What is meant by the karma of the functional activity of phenomena?
The distinct functions of the eye, ear, and so forth— the Buddha’s teaching on the three karmas is profound and subtle; relying upon reason and scripture, I have composed this elegant exposition.
May I, by virtue of this merit, deliver all sentient beings, causing them all to swiftly realize pure awakening.
Treatise on the Establishment of Karma in the Mahāyāna, One Scroll.
